extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, intellectual property firms, patent draftsmen, and individual inventors working on design patents for digital interfaces, icons, holograms, and projections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing USPTO-compliant design patent drawings and related specification/claim strategy for computer-generated images, icons, interfaces, holograms, and projections under the USPTO's 2026 supplemental examination guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must be ornamental and embodied in an article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents, governed by 35 U.S.C. § 171, require that a design be 'ornamental' and 'embodied in an article of manufacture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory requirement remains: the design must be embodied in an article of manufacture. For computer-generated images, the article of manufacture may be the computer, the display screen, or even a tangible medium on which the image is stored or displayed. The application must tie the design to some tangible article even if the article is not drawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated electronic images may be claimed without depicting a physical device
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may present the design as a computer-generated electronic image (e.g., an icon or interface) shown alone, without any surrounding physical device in the drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must make clear that this image is embodied in an article of manufacture. Showing the image alone allows applicants to capture the true ornamental essence without being boxed in by hardware, but lines and shapes must precisely define scope since there is no physical frame for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holograms and projections are explicitly patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance states that 'computer-generated interfaces' include projections and holograms, permitting protection of floating or projected UI elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be eligible, the hologram or projection must be separate from the computer, display, or system that generates it and must be more than a transient or disembodied picture or three-dimensional image. Drawings may need to show the image in its environment using broken lines to indicate unclaimed structures (e.g., a windshield or room).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines (dashed lines) indicate environmental structure not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines may be used to show environmental structure that is not part of the claimed design (e.g., room walls, floor, ceiling, device outlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new guidance clarifies flexible use of broken lines for computer-generated designs. Show the claimed design in solid lines and environmental or supporting structures in broken lines. Mastery of what to render in solid versus broken lines is critical to defining scope and complying with USPTO conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must explicitly describe the article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Because drawings may depict less physical context, the specification must explicitly describe the article of manufacture in which the design is embodied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on the drawings to meet the article-of-manufacture requirement. A well-drafted specification should tie the design to tangible articles (computer, display, medium) even when the drawings are standalone images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination focuses on whether the design is directed to a statutory article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will assess whether the design is embodied in an article of manufacture rather than treating presentation rules as determinative or allowing abstract claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentational flexibility does not change statutory eligibility. Ensure claims and specification demonstrate that the design is not an abstract concept but is tied to a tangible article of manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose presentation: standalone image versus environmental context
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must choose whether to show the design as a standalone image or with environmental context (e.g., device, room).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broken lines to disclaim structures you do not wish to claim. Consider which presentation best captures the ornamental essence and strategic breadth you want. Removing unnecessary physical structures can broaden scope, but choose views carefully to fully define the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show all perspectives necessary to fully define the design
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must show enough views to completely disclose the ornamental appearance of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standalone images may require fewer views than device-attached drawings, but applicants must still show all perspectives needed to define the design. A skilled draftsman can determine the optimal number and type of views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess design qualifying factors before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before pursuing a design patent, confirm the design is ornamental, new, original, and embodied in an article of manufacture; for holograms, ensure it is more than a transient image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical checklist: confirm novelty and ornamentality and that the design can be tied to an article of manufacture. For holograms/projections, ensure the claimed subject is separate from generating hardware and persistent enough to qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and clarity of lines and shapes are paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawings show the claimed subject alone (no physical frame), the clarity and precision of lines and shapes must precisely define the scope of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a device frame to constrain meaning, every line matters—imprecise rendering can unintentionally narrow or fail to capture intended features. High-quality, precise drawings improve enforceability and examination outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with experienced patent draftsmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing quality and strategic choices (views, broken lines, framing) materially affect the scope and compliance of design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage draftsmen experienced with USPTO conventions and the new guidance to select views, apply broken lines appropriately, and ensure drawings and specification align with examination standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisit pending applications to take advantage of new guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending design patent applications for computer-generated interfaces, icons, or related subject matter should be reviewed in light of the guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some instances, it may be possible to file a continuation or request to amend drawings to remove unnecessary physical structures and thereby broaden protection. Evaluate existing portfolios for opportunities to update drawings or claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize number of views versus cost and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a design patent for a standalone image may require fewer views, potentially reducing cost, but views must suffice to define the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance cost savings with the need to show all perspectives necessary to avoid gaps in protection. A patent draftsman can recommend the optimal set of views for coverage and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use broken lines to show environmental context for holograms/projections
rubrics_metrics.description: For holographic or projected designs, show environment elements (windshield, room, vehicle HUD) in broken lines to indicate they are not part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates how the design appears in situ while preserving claim focus on the holographic/projection element. Broken-line environmental depiction helps clarify what is claimed vs. not claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a layered IP strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents are one tool among others; applicants should consider layering design protection with utility patents, copyrights, and trademarks for digital products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For software and digital assets, combine design patents (visual ornamentation) with utility patents (functional aspects), copyright (creative content/code), and trademark (branding) to maximize protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on device outlines in prior art-limiting ways
rubrics_metrics.description: Past practice of showing a device even when not claimed often unintentionally constrained protection; new guidance permits avoiding that limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing unnecessary device outlines can broaden scope, but ensure the specification still ties the design to an article of manufacture and that drawings remain sufficiently descriptive.
